title: Young Men Steadily Catch Up to Young Women in Online Appearance Anxiety
author: Petrova, Karina
summary: A five-year longitudinal study from Griffith University finds that young men who began adolescence with minimal appearance anxiety steadily converged with their female peers until moderate-to-high online appearance preoccupation became statistically universal. The screen functions as a democratizing anxiety machine. What was once a female-specific vulnerability rooted in cultural messaging about physical appearance has generalized into an anthropological condition of perpetual digital surveillance and comparison.
points: Young men who started with low appearance anxiety steadily converged with anxious female peers until online appearance preoccupation became universal.
The screen is a democratizing anxiety machine that erases gender differences in appearance preoccupation over a five-year period.
What was once a female-specific vulnerability tied to cultural messaging about women's worth has generalized to both sexes through digital platforms.
The digital mirror without an off-switch subjects everyone to perpetual comparative evaluation, producing anxiety across genders.
When the mirror is always on and always comparative, everyone eventually flinches at their own reflection.
quotes: Young men who began adolescence with little concern about their digital appearance steadily converged with their more anxious female peers.
The screen is a democratizing anxiety machine.
What was once a female-specific vulnerability, rooted in cultural messaging that tied women's worth to their physical appearance, has now been generalized as an anthropological condition.
When the mirror is always on and always comparative, everyone eventually flinches.” Archived from PsyPost on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
